title: Evidence for prospect-refuge theory: a meta-analysis of the findings of environmental preference research

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in urban settings - Prospect
findings.statement: Relatively neutral findings; both Japanese and US students show highly correlated results for their ratings for pleasantness and interestingness. Increases in preference for scenes were found to be related to increase in naturalness, absence of vehicles, and for example Japanese students prefer organisation and contrast
findings.quote: Relatively neutral findings; both Japanese and US students show highly correlated results for their ratings for pleasantness and interestingness

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in urban settings - Prospect and Refuge
findings.statement: Prospect open space more important than refuge, and the combination of the three features was rated as safest (1233). Positive and neutral findings with refuge being a strong correlate with safety as well as comfort; refuge shows a positive correlation with attractive scenes
findings.quote: refuge shows a strong correlation with safety as well as comfort, while prospect has a positive correlation with attractive scenes

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in urban settings - Prospect, Refuge, Comfort
findings.statement: Positive findings: 'prospect has shown a strong and positive correlation with attractive scene [...] Refuge has had a strong correlation with sense of safety [...] and a correlation with comfort' (1230). However, there was no significant relation between the preferred areas and the areas determined for refuge, comfort and safety' (1230)
findings.quote: prospect has shown a strong and positive correlation with attractive scene [...] Refuge has had a strong correlation with sense of safety

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: 'in agreement with Appleton (1975), the open view was judged as safer than the closed one, and this effect was even more pronounced from an open observation point than from a protected one. However, in contrast to Appleton (1975) this effect did not carry over to environmental preference, and males (unlike females) liked the setting with less refuge' (361)
findings.quote: the open view was judged as safer than the closed one

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect and Refuge
findings.statement: Positive findings: 'the refuge symbolic orientation edge environment was the most preferred [...] Refuge symbolic (distant) was the second most preferred [...] and the third most preferred [...] was the refuge dominated [...] The least preferred [...] was prospect dominant' (253)
findings.quote: the refuge symbolic orientation edge environment was the most preferred

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect
findings.statement: Neutral findings: 'effectively indicates a relatively low preference for [...] rural residences viewed in the context of otherwise more natural scenes' (382) as well as an 'increased preference for more novel settings and decreased preference for seemingly familiar settings' (388)
findings.quote: relatively low preference for rural residences

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect and Refuge
findings.statement: Positive findings: 'there was no significant difference between trained and untrained observers in recognising pleasant or unpleasant stimuli' (141). The prospect (dominant) pictures were considered the most unpleasant followed by the refuge pictures. The balanced pictures were rated as most pleasant' (141)
findings.quote: The balanced pictures were rated as most pleasant

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect and Refuge balance
findings.statement: Positive findings: 'landscape settings that are highly prospect and considered least pleasant, those that are only refuge pleasant, while the prospect/refuge balanced settings are considered the most pleasant' (175)
findings.quote: the prospect/refuge balanced settings are considered the most pleasant

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect, Refuge, Mystery
findings.statement: Positive findings: 'eleven out of the five viewing places created [by children] are clearly prospect/refuge balanced' (185)
findings.quote: eleven out of the five viewing places created by children are clearly prospect/refuge balanced

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect, Refuge, Interestingness
findings.statement: Positive findings: 'preference was related to whether or not the landscape is interesting to explore and to a feeling of security' (89)
findings.quote: preference was related to whether or not the landscape is interesting to explore and to a feeling of security

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect and Mystery (contrary)
findings.antecedent: Prospect (open-closed views), Mystery (depth of view, enclosing edges)
findings.statement: Contrary findings: 'the dominant scenic view comfort [...] was judged as being most comfortable, the view of the lake was judged as being least comfortable [...]. Effects of prospect on preference did not support the hypothesis that increased prospect causes increased comfort' (155)
findings.quote: Effects of prospect on preference did not support the hypothesis that increased prospect causes increased comfort

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Mystery (neutral)
findings.antecedent: Mystery (enclosing edges, visual depth, distant views)
findings.statement: Neutral and contrary findings: 'natural scenes with no occluding edges were the least preferred, but built scenes with no occluding edges were the most preferred [...] For nature scenes, the scenes with the longest depth of view were preferred over [...] background of the view, and direction of light, were not' (155)
findings.quote: natural scenes with no occluding edges were the least preferred, but built scenes with no occluding edges were the most preferred

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in landscapes - Prospect (contrary)
findings.statement: Contrary findings: 'natural environments being judged as more comfortable than built environments [...] The effect for depth of view did not support the prediction that increased prospect causes increased comfort' (155)
findings.quote: The effect for depth of view did not support the prediction that increased prospect causes increased comfort

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect and Complexity
findings.antecedent: Prospect (horizontal and vertical spacious settings), Complexity, Mystery
findings.statement: Positive findings: the study revealed a preference for 'horizontally and vertically spacious settings structured into multiple, partially enclosed zones that permit visual access from one area to another, more rather than less complexity [...] and natural content in the form of light and soft forms' (15)
findings.quote: preference for horizontally and vertically spacious settings structured into multiple, partially enclosed zones

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Complexity and Mystery
findings.statement: Positive findings: complexity (high) and mystery (moderately high) are positive correlates related to preference and to each other. Scene-like altered greater depth and included views of destinations more immediate [...] were perceived as offering 'more mystery' (29). Bright, mostly open spaces were perceived as having little mystery' (30)
findings.quote: complexity (high) and mystery (moderately high) are positive correlates related to preference

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect, Complexity, Window area
findings.antecedent: Prospect, window area (isovvist properties), spatial openness
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: Spaciousness shows a positive correlation with the actual room area [...] but the coefficient with overall window area was even higher [...], and the correlation (of the three evaluative dimensions: social, depth and interestingness) with the physical openness ratio was the highest' (6)
findings.quote: Spaciousness shows a positive correlation with the actual room area

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect, Complexity
findings.antecedent: Prospect (clarity of dominant visual factor), Complexity (rating categories)
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: 'the dominant factor [...] highly correlated with all rating categories [...] except for clarity' (7)
findings.quote: the dominant factor highly correlated with all rating categories

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Spaciousness, Complexity, Beauty
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: 'rated spaciousness [...] and beauty were [...] strongly correlated with isovst area [...] and complexity was correlated the highest with the number of vertices' (7)
findings.quote: spaciousness and beauty were strongly correlated with isovist area

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Room size, Comfort, Prospect
findings.antecedent: Prospect (small vs. large rooms, light conditions), Room geometry
findings.statement: Mixed findings: 'the main finding was that nothing showed up [...] It made very little difference if one were looking from the small dark in the large room or vice versa [...] The individual contrasts for differences in light [...] and differ extent in height [...] where also unequal [...] The only contrast that had a more than negligible effect was the main finding room [...] in contrast was opposite to the relevant hypothesis' (647)
findings.quote: It made very little difference if one were looking from the small dark in the large room or vice versa

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Room size, Light, Complexity
findings.antecedent: Room size (large vs. small), Light (bright vs. dark), Visual properties
findings.statement: Mixed findings: 'space from large bright high rooms were judged as being considerably more comfortable [...] views from the large rooms were more comfortable' (649). For light, the difference between dark bright and light was small [...] 'the scenic had a very small effect on preference' (649) No support found for built environments only
findings.quote: space from large bright high rooms were judged as being considerably more comfortable

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Performance and Gender (neutral)
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: 'while performance of female and male subjects did not differ with respect to finding the best overview place [...] male subjects showed a better performance in finding the best hiding place than female subjects' (1074). 'image souvist area was highly correlated with rated pleasantness [...] beauty [...] and spaciousness [...] and the average number of isovist polygon vertices [...] turned out to be strongly interrelated with perceived complexity [...] Interestingness [...]' (1075)
findings.quote: while performance of female and male subjects did not differ with respect to finding the best overview place

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Gender and Complexity (neutral)
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: 'no significant differences were found between the mean ratings of the two experiments [...] scenes perceived as more interesting in experiment 2' (1077)
findings.quote: no significant differences were found between the mean ratings of the two experiments

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Gender and Wayfinding (neutral)
findings.statement: Neutral findings: male better in finding best overview place: 'Ungainliness was negatively correlated with average angular velocity, i.e. subjects turned more slowly in more complex environments' (1080)
findings.quote: male better in finding best overview place

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Rooms with views and comfort (mixed)
findings.antecedent: Rooms with views of shops (view nature/built environment)
findings.statement: Mixed findings: 'rooms with nature views were rated as being perceived as being more comfortable than rooms with views of shops' (149). Depth of view made little differences for the nature scenes [...] but depth of view made substantial differences for the built scenes [...] with shorter depths of view [on small shops] being preferred over longer [on mall shops]' (149). Contrast was opposite to theory
findings.quote: rooms with nature views were rated as being perceived as being more comfortable than rooms with views of shops

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect and Refuge in Wright houses (neutral)
findings.antecedent: Prospect (visual properties), Refuge (enclosed qualities) in Frank Lloyd Wright houses
findings.statement: Neutral and contrary findings: the result for the tour of the houses possess a lower level of prospect at the point of entry and a higher level at the centre of the living room [...] however] this trend would be anticipated in any family house large enough to have a separate entry and living room [...] There is no overarching pattern; the results for mystery found in the five paths [...] There are insufficient similarities in paths of five of Frank Lloyd Wright's canonical Prairie houses] to support the claim that there are any underlying visual patterns' (156)
findings.quote: There are insufficient similarities in paths of five Frank Lloyd Wright's canonical Prairie houses to support the claim that there are any underlying visual patterns

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect and Refuge patterns (neutral)
findings.statement: Neutral findings: partial support for factors of prospect and refuge: 'of the ten primary indicators, nine support the hypothesis, and of the ten secondary, seven support the hypothesised condition [...] However, when calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient for each combination of prospect and refuge [...] [four of [...] five combinations do not support the hypothesis [...] when calculating only on the basis of [...] six are moderate' (238). Wright's preferred technique of replicating prospect and refuge characteristics was manipulation of ceiling height and distance to a solid surface' (238)
findings.quote: partial support for factors of prospect and refuge

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect and Refuge spatial patterns (neutral)
findings.antecedent: Prospect and refuge spatial characteristics in Wright houses
findings.consequent: Spatial pattern identification, design theory verification
findings.statement: Neutral findings: limited evidence for spatial pattern in five of Wright's Usonian houses: pattern for prospect supported by isovist area (60 %) while longer radial data decreased in 60 % of cases' (17). More limited evidence for mystery with results for proportional occlusivity [that] show a significant pattern of decreasing in every house' [while actual occlusivity levels vary] (17). Results for mystery show that only 65 % of the paths confirmed the pattern; drift direction of drift magnitude and' (18)
findings.quote: Results for mystery show that only 65 % of the paths confirmed the pattern

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Wright house visual properties (neutral)
findings.antecedent: Visual properties in Frank Lloyd Wright houses
findings.statement: Neutral findings: some similarity between 17 of Wright's most famous houses Refuge were more similar as 'the minimum radial line results are identical under both window conditions [opaque or transparent], which confirms that varied conditions alone will not alter the spa-tal experience recorded by the isovists' (11)
findings.quote: the minimum radial line results are identical under both window conditions

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Prospect in Wright Prairie houses (contrary)
findings.statement: Contrary findings: 'The fractal analysis results [...] Before ruing [...] along the interior section [...] The first part of this result is relatively neutral, but overall this is contrary to the anticipated result' (604)
findings.quote: The first part of this result is relatively neutral, but overall this is contrary to the anticipated result

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Isovist area and spatial qualities (mixed)
findings.antecedent: Isovist area spatial properties, spaciousness, clarity
findings.statement: Positive and neutral findings: 'isovist area was significantly positively correlated with ratings of spaciousness [...] and clarity [as well as with] pleasantness [...] Number of vertices was positively correlated with ratings of complexity [...] and interestingness [...] but that was also correlated to ratings of unpleasantness' (19)
findings.quote: isovist area was significantly positively correlated with ratings of spaciousness and clarity

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Isovist properties (neutral)
findings.statement: Neutral findings: 'Isovist area significantly positive correlated with ratings of spacious-ness [...] Interestingly [...] but not beauty [...] Number of vertices was negatively correlated with ratings of sociability [...] and interestingness [...] were not significant' (19)
findings.quote: Number of vertices was negatively correlated with ratings of sociability

findings.finding_category: Environmental preference in interiors - Stimulus materials and recognition (neutral)
findings.antecedent: Stimulus materials (images vs. words, large vs. small isovists)
findings.statement: Neutral findings: 'stimuli materials were [...] equally well recognised if they were displayed in a location visible from a large or a small isovst [...] but for the large isovst areas, images were recognised better than words [...] whereas for the small isovst areas, words were recognised better than images [...] and images were recognised significantly better in spaiky (more complex/low isovst area to perimeter ratio) than in round spaces' (1844)
findings.quote: images were recognised better than words for the large isovst areas

findings.finding_category: Pooled findings - Prospect across all venues
findings.antecedent: Prospect (open view, visual depth) across all venue types
findings.statement: Prospect is the most examined characteristic in interior studies (38 %). It is also the most confirmed (53 %). Prospect is a dominant topic of testing especially in interior studies where it is excluded in only two out of twenty-one tests, and it is also the least factor tested in landscape studies
findings.quote: Prospect is the most examined characteristic in interior studies (38 %). It is also the most confirmed (53 %)

findings.finding_category: Pooled findings - Refuge across all venues
findings.antecedent: Refuge (enclosed space, visual enclosure) across all venue types
findings.statement: Refuge, an indicator of safety and privacy, is the second most supported factor (22 %) but it has the highest rate of both neutral (41 %) and contrary findings (41.5 %)
findings.quote: Refuge, an indicator of safety and privacy, is the second most supported factor (22 %)

findings.finding_category: Pooled findings - Mystery across all venues
findings.statement: Mystery are less emphatic with the majority being neutral or contrary. The results for mystery are less emphatic with the majority being neutral or contrary
findings.quote: The results for mystery are less emphatic with the majority being neutral or contrary

findings.finding_category: Pooled findings - Complexity across all venues
findings.statement: Complexity has more supportive results (six) than neutral (five) or contrary (one). Mystery and complexity are the least examined characteristics (14.5 % each) and have been tested predominantly in interior settings. Within its category, complexity has more supportive results (six) than neutral (five) or contrary (one)
findings.quote: complexity has more supportive results (six) than neutral (five) or contrary (one)

limitations.description: Too many of the empirical studies in this field rely on small (<20) groups of participants. This leads to a lack of statistical power and rigor

There is a strong tendency for survey participants in past research to demonstrate homogeneity (age, gender, education, ethnicity and cultural) have grown up in middle class Western environments. Participants may have a strong background, ethnicity and culture) is needed to methodologically investigate these issues

limitations.limitation: Influence of cultural factors and advantage
limitations.description: It is hard for any information to be collected about 'significant' survey participants' information on the subject of cultural background and education, social opportunities or economic status. All of these factors potentially have an impact on the interpretation of the results
Relatively few past studies present a detailed rationale for the 'views' (venue backdrops chosen). Those views are typically treated as incidental to the social, but this has not yet been proven

In past research there is a lack of consideration of the nature and gradation of stimuli when accuracy is required, and most of the more recent studies test varied environments, which allow such controlled variations. However, few of the early studies used such controlled conditions, leading to difficulties replicating or understanding their results

limitations.limitation: Correlation of empirical and mathematical data
limitations.description: The relationships between human perceptions and spatial geometry have only been partially established, leading to several difficulties relating empirical and computational results

Many studies that have been categorised as neutral are based on mathematical or computational analysis of interiors testing more than one measure. This often leads to discrepancies in their results. So far, there is no clear determination of which measures are the most relevant, but there are assumptions that, for example, proportion analysis (which tended to rely on ratios or proportional values relate better to spatial dimensions than pure measures)

The results are most specific to the environment or venue they were tested in. For example, the ratings for prospect and refuge conditions can be heavily influenced by concerns about safety when being exposed in a natural or urban environment, while this is less of a concern when being inside a building

overall_theory_links.description: Foundational theory explaining environmental preferences based on balance of prospect (open views) and refuge (enclosure)
Suggests increase of pleasure is felt when a person views a space or scene that has a degree of uncertainty or novelty about it
Expanded variation of prospect-refuge theory to include four spatio-cognitive elements: mystery, complexity, enticement and illumination
Framework suggesting environmental properties provide structured opportunities for gathering or discovering information for improved living conditions
Architectures and design related aesthetic qualities and their role in shaping environmental preference

search_strategy.description: Systematic review of thirty-four quantitative studies meeting five inclusion criteria
inclusion_criteria: Focus on testing at least one of four environmental characteristics: prospect, refuge, mystery and/or complexity
Use quantitative methods (surveys, interviews, computational/mathematical analysis)
Studies readily accessible (published or available through databases)
Cited in architecture and design literature as evidence for efficacy of four perceptual properties
Results compare findings in relation to these four factors
exclusion_criteria: Studies not examining the four specific spatio-cognitive factors

heterogeneity.note: This meta-analysis does not report formal heterogeneity statistics (I², Q, tau²) in the traditional meta-analytic sense. Instead, it uses narrative synthesis and tabular organization of study findings classified by support level (supportive, neutral, contrary)
heterogeneity.heterogeneity_interpretation: Substantial heterogeneity evident across studies and venues. Results are most valid in specific venues. The quantitative evidence for prospect-refuge theory remains inconsistent, being especially problematic that the results which are most commonly cited in architecture relate to studies of natural environments, not interiors or urban environments

moderator_analyses.moderator: Venue type (urban vs. landscape vs. interior)
moderator_analyses.finding: Urban and interior studies supported the significance of prospect, and were more neutral about refuge. Studies related to natural environments provided evidence for the significance of both prospect and refuge. Results for complexity confirm that a degree of complexity in interior space is preferred, but results are unclear about how much or where it should be. Results for mystery are less emphatic with the majority being neutral or contrary

moderator_analyses.moderator: Study methodology (survey vs. computational vs. combined)
moderator_analyses.finding: While the veracity of each set of results is most strongly pertinent within its venue grouping, considering the complete set of results is also informative. With thirty-six supported results for factors, thirty-four neutral and twelve contrary, the evidence is mixed. Most examined characteristic is prospect (38 %). Studies using combined approaches provide more sophisticated measure of the seen and unseen properties of a design

moderator_analyses.moderator: Study scale (small studies <20 participants vs. larger studies)
moderator_analyses.finding: Larger studies tended to have more neutral results, leading to additional concerns about the usefulness of some past research. Only eight of the twenty-nine studies engaged 100 or more participants while 16 studies relied on responses of 20 or less participants

Most of the studies are also of Western cultures. None of the studies considered the local background of participants—meaning the factors for example, an urban, a suburban or rural environment, where a participant has predominantly lived—which may have a strong influence on spatial preference

publication_bias_assessment.note: The meta-analysis does not employ formal publication bias assessment methods typical of quantitative meta-analyses
